account:
This node is a self-contained compilation task that draws exclusively on the writer's own general knowledge (the dossier explicitly says no source materials are provided and to rely on general knowledge while flagging uncertainty). The acceptance condition is mechanical and checkable: 4–6 items, each with a one-line claim plus a short accurate description, every uncertain item flagged, no invented statistics, quotations, exhibitions, or proper names. Context is complete because the dossier fixes the audience, genre, stance, and constraints, and nothing here depends on a sibling's future output. Expanding would only re-partition a trivial knowledge list; expansion_required is false and the remaining budget is better preserved. I therefore solve in place and deliver the stock below.

GROUNDED REFERENTS: categories named in the objective (current AI 'slop'; recognizable default AI look; older human-made kitsch; photography vs painting; recorded music vs live performance). No proper names, no invented specifics.

ASSEMBLED STOCK (5 items)
1. CURRENT AI 'SLOP' — Claim: the current glut of machine-generated 'slop' on social feeds and stock libraries is the most visible face of AI kitsch today. Description: on popular social and stock-photo feeds one now sees endless repetitions of one template — smooth-furred animals posed face-on, idealized mothers cradling infants, sunlit cottages empty of people — each carrying pleasing light, balanced symmetry, and a soft emotion with nothing underneath to reward a second look. FLAGGED: 'slop' is a contested, non-technical label; I describe a widely observed impression, not a formally defined category.
2. THE DEFAULT AI LOOK — Claim: machine images have a recognizable house style — glossy, hyper-smooth, faintly plastic — that viewers now clock in seconds. Description: generated pictures tend to be over-detailed and hollow at once: strand-by-strand hair and fur, glistening highlights, occasionally wrong hands, a wet, oiled-plastic texture. The uniformity comes less from any artist than from the statistical center of training data pulling every output toward the most common, least surprising combination. FLAGGED: the 'oily look' is a repeated lay observation, not a measured property, and I can't vouch for specific models' training recipes.
3. OLDER HUMAN-MADE KITSCH — Claim: long before AI, human workshops mass-produced similar kitsch in sentimental calendar and greeting-card art. Description: for much of the twentieth century, small firms and studios churned out rain-slicked streets, fly-fishing grandfathers, and mournful puppies — technically smooth, instantly legible, engineered to please and nothing more. Contemporaries already accused this assembly-line sentiment of substituting stock emotion for genuine feeling, much as earlier formulaic academic painting had been. FLAGGED: the genres and their criticism are real, but I won't name a specific artist, catalog, or exhibition for risk of error.
4. PHOTOGRAPHY VS PAINTING — Claim: photography's arrival brought cries that machine-made images would cheapen and destroy true painting. Description: around the mid-nineteenth century, painters and critics feared a lens-and-chemical process that copied the world faster and more faithfully than any hand would render representational art redundant and superficial. Instead, photography pushed painting away from straight imitation toward impression, expression, and abstraction — a standing rebuke to 'this kills art' talk. FLAGGED: I date the reaction to the 1830s–1850s but won't pin exact dates or quote the loudest detractors from memory.
5. RECORDED MUSIC VS LIVE PERFORMANCE — Claim: recorded music stirred parallel fears that a copyable artifact would end live, present-tense music. Description: when early recordings appeared around the turn of the twentieth century, some performers and writers worried that people would stop attending concerts and mistake the fixed, repeatable record for the living moment. As with photography, real dislocation occurred yet was selective: recording reshaped the art far more than it annihilated it. FLAGGED: the specific contemporary anxieties and who voiced them are recollection, not verified quotation.

These five span both sides of the argument (none pre-slanted), mix present and past, and each carries an explicit uncertainty marker where accuracy is not guaranteed.
